statement: Among US Army enlisted men who served in Vietnam in 1970–1971, narcotic use and self-reported addiction were common, but few of the men addicted there were addicted again after they came home, and by the principal investigator's account treatment did not explain this; she also says that the conditions in Vietnam were unlike anything before. In her later account, 45% of Army enlisted men in Vietnam in 1970–71 tried narcotics (34% heroin, 38% opium) and 20% said they had felt strung out or addicted there, claims the researchers accepted after asking about frequency and length of use and about withdrawal symptoms; heroin there was cheap, pure and did not have to be injected, more than 80% of men were offered it, usually within a week of arrival, and those who became addicted had typically begun early in their tour, before exposure to combat (Robins, 1993). In the study's first report, of 451 men interviewed from a random sample of 470 who left Vietnam in September 1971, 43% had used narcotics there; of these 196 men, 46% said they had been addicted (47% by the study's own criteria: at least three of more-than-weekly use for over a month, two or more of four withdrawal symptoms, withdrawal lasting at least two days or 12 hours if eased, and believing oneself addicted), which is 20% of all the men (21% by the criteria), against 0.2% (0.4%) before Vietnam and 0.7% (1%) in the 8 to 12 months after return, when 10% had used a narcotic (Robins et al., 1975). Of the men addicted in Vietnam, 5% were addicted in the first year after return and 12% at any time in the 3 years after return, usually briefly (Robins, 1993); the first report's figure, read approximately, shows about 2% of 90 such men in the random sample and about 7% of 341 in a second sample, selected on a positive urine test at departure, addicted 8 to 10 months after return, and how the 5% combines the samples is not stated. The lecture's text also gives '6% overall' re-addicted, without a time frame, but its own Figure 6 shows about 12%, matching the three-year figure, which is the one used here. Many men used narcotics again without becoming addicted again: nearly half of those addicted in Vietnam tried narcotics again after return, by the text (about 6 in 10 in Figure 6, read approximately), and of those who used heroin regularly about half were re-addicted (Robins, 1993); of 134 men still addicted when they left Vietnam (both samples, unweighted), 50% used a narcotic in the months after return and 14% were addicted again; and the first report gives 7% of the men who used narcotics after return becoming addicted, against about half of those who used them in Vietnam (Robins et al., 1975; in the random sample about 3 of some 45 men, editors' calculation on the study card). A third of the men addicted in Vietnam received even simple detoxification in service, and after return fewer than 2% of the men who had used narcotics in Vietnam, 6% of men positive at departure and 14% of those positive at departure who kept using entered drug treatment; men who did enter treatment relapsed as often as young civilians treated at the federal narcotics hospital in Lexington, two-thirds by the time of interview, and the principal investigator reads treated cases as people who cannot stop on their own; and among the men who used narcotics again, none of the factors tested predicted who became addicted again, including behaviour problems before service, which had predicted narcotic use in Vietnam, parents' problems, drug use in Vietnam, IQ, combat and demographic characteristics (Robins, 1993). The men were young enlisted soldiers from one month's departures, in a setting where, she writes, never before had so many young men been addicted to opiates without the usual risk factors and where few of them would have become addicted had they stayed in the US; addiction was self-reported, checked against military records (97% of men whose records showed narcotic use reported it) and urine taken at interview; the lecture gives no total sample size, no definition of re-addiction and no intervals, several of its text figures differ from its graphs, and its three-year figures could not be checked against the three-year report, which was not read; and the first report leaves open whether the men's backgrounds or the change of setting explains the recovery. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Did the soldiers addicted to heroin in Vietnam stay addicted? Mostly not. In Vietnam in 1970 and 1971, almost half of US Army enlisted men tried narcotics, mostly heroin or opium, and 20 in 100 said they had been addicted there; heroin was cheap, pure and could be smoked. Of the men who had been addicted, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year back home and 12 in 100 at some point within 3 years, usually briefly. Many used narcotics again without becoming addicted again. Few entered treatment after coming home: fewer than 2 in 100 of the men who had used narcotics in Vietnam did, and those who did relapsed about as often as civilian patients. The researcher who led the study says the situation was unlike anything before: never had so many young men been addicted without the usual risk factors, and few of them would have become addicted at home. The figures are the men's own reports, checked against military records and urine tests; the later ones come from her lecture, which gives no total numbers and whose text and graphs differ in places.
population: US Army enlisted men (no officers, no women) who left Vietnam for the United States in September 1971, half of them under 21 on arrival in Vietnam: a random general sample of 470 (451 interviewed) and a random sample of 495 of the about 1,400 whose departure urine was positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates (898 of the 943 selected interviewed 8 to 12 months after return); about 3 years after departure, 94% of the men first interviewed were interviewed again
exposure: Narcotic use (heroin or opium) and self-reported addiction in Vietnam in 1970–71, where heroin was cheap, pure, widely offered and could be smoked; addiction self-reported and checked against frequency and length of use and withdrawal symptoms (in the first report also by the study's own criteria)
comparator: The same men before service and after return (no comparison group for remission); the lecture contrasts young civilian patients treated at the federal narcotics hospital in Lexington (another study)
outcome: Addiction again after return, as self-reported: in the 8 to 12 months after return (first report) and in the first year and at any time in the 3 years after return (lecture); narcotic use after return; entry into drug treatment after return
magnitude: Robins (1993): in Vietnam 45% tried narcotics (34% heroin, 38% opium), 20% reported addiction; of men addicted in Vietnam, addicted again in the first year after return 5%, at any time in 3 years 12% (the text also gives '6% overall', with no time frame; Figure 6 about 12%, measured by the editors); after return nearly half (text) or about 61% (Figure 6) used narcotics, about 43% heroin and about 23% regularly (Figure 6, approximate), and about half of the men who used heroin regularly were re-addicted; simple detoxification in service for a third of men addicted in Vietnam; drug treatment after return for under 2% of men who used narcotics in Vietnam, 6% of men positive at departure and 14% of those positive at departure who kept using; two-thirds of treated men relapsed by the time of interview. Robins et al. (1975), general sample N = 451, before Vietnam / in Vietnam / since return: narcotics 11% / 43% / 10%; addiction by self-report 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%; of the 196 who used narcotics in Vietnam, 46% (self-report) and 47% (criteria) addicted; 7% of the men who used narcotics after return became addicted (about 3 of 45 in the general sample, editors' calculation on the card); men first addicted in Vietnam addicted again 8 to 10 months after return about 2% (N = 90, general sample) and about 7% (N = 341, urine-positive sample), read approximately from the figure; still addicted at departure (N = 134, both samples, unweighted): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% addicted again; stated remission rate 95% (no denominator).

evidence.locator: Why the study was a technical success, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 1042, right column); The study's assets, (C) and (E) (p. 1043)
evidence.extracted: Two samples of Army enlisted men who left Vietnam in September 1971, the first month urine screening ran throughout the country: one from the Department of Defense active-duty roster and one from the Surgeon General's records of men positive at departure, used to over-sample men who used heroin (over 600 men who used narcotics in Vietnam were interviewed) and weighted back to their share of the population; matched draft-eligible civilians as a comparison group. 96% were interviewed when back 8 to 12 months, and 94% of them again 3 years after departure; 97% of men whose military record showed narcotic use reported it, and urine taken at the end of each interview showed no more current use than the men had reported. Draftees typically reached Vietnam at about 19 and were discharged at 20 or 21.

evidence.extracted: The authors leave open whether the background characteristics that distinguish the returnees from the typical person addicted to narcotics in the United States, or the change in the social setting of use between Vietnam and the United States, explains the high remission; they do not know how much the short tour of duty contributed; they judge concealment unlikely (the men's candour, their free discussion of drug use in Vietnam, a low rate of urine specimens positive for opiates, high interview completion); they name Vietnam as a locale atypical in danger and in the quality, price and availability of its drugs, and the sample as homogeneous in age, sex, occupation and period, so the findings may not apply elsewhere; and new cases emerged throughout the period after return.

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the claim as worded. The first-year figures are primary data from random samples of one month's returnees, 95% interviewed, with self-reports checked against military records and urine taken at interview, by interviewers who did not know which men had used drugs (card sc_robins_1975: JBI moderate); concealment would lower the figures for use after return, and the authors judge it unlikely. The three-year figures, the treatment figures and Figure 6 come from the principal investigator's lecture (card sc_robins_1993: narrative-review checklist, high), which gives no total sample size, no definition of re-addiction and no intervals, and whose text and graphs disagree in places ('6% overall' against about 12% in Figure 6; 'nearly half' against about 61% using narcotics again); the statement gives the figures with their stated time frames and names the disagreements. Read strictly, the lecture-only figures would be rated down one level, to very low.

inconsistency.note: The 1975 report and the 1993 lecture describe one study and agree in direction; their differences (43% against 45% trying narcotics; about 2% and 7% in the two samples against 5% combined in the first year; 95% against 96% interviewed) lie within one study's reporting and are stated.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: young US Army enlisted men in Vietnam in 1970–71 and after return; the statement gives the principal investigator's own caution that the conditions were unprecedented and that few of the men would have become addicted at home, so nothing is generalized to people who become addicted in ordinary civilian life.

imprecision.note: No intervals are printed and some counts are small (about 2 of 90 men in the random sample's figure; 14% of 134), but the share re-addicted stays small in every figure (about 2% to 14% of men addicted in Vietnam, by sample and time frame).

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a single cohort; the three-year report (Robins et al., 1980) and the later follow-ups were not read.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim (proportions in one cohort): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS 6.3); not downgraded (see the domain notes): low. Strict reading: the three-year re-addiction, the treatment figures and the regular-use figure come only from the principal investigator's lecture and alone would be very low. Status single study: the 1975 report and the 1993 lecture describe one cohort and are counted once. The comparison with civilian patients at Lexington is with another study's treated population, not a control group, and is reported as the author's contrast; the matched civilian comparison group the lecture describes gives no figures here. The claim describes what happened to these men; it does not say why (the first report leaves open the men's backgrounds or the change of setting), and the treatment figures describe who entered treatment, not what treatment did. Not used: the lecture's '6% overall' (no time frame; its own figure shows about 12%), and Heyman's (2013) restatement of these figures, which joins numbers for different groups and time spans.

verification.flag_note: Question 3 of reader 752 in round pdf-2026-11-26 (who gets addicted, and who recovers). Not read, and each could change the figures: Robins, Davis & Nurco (1974, American Journal of Public Health 64 supplement; no DOI recorded), the source of the 5% first-year figure; Robins et al. (1980, 'Vietnam veterans three years after Vietnam', book chapter), the three-year report behind the 12% and the regular-use figures; Robins (1974), the monograph with the full first-year data; Price et al. (2001) and the later follow-ups of the same men (Ledgerwood et al., 2008; Price et al., 2009, as Heyman describes them); Hall & Weier (2016, a methodological appraisal). The lecture's text and graphs disagree in three places (6% against about 12% re-addicted; nearly half against about 61% using narcotics again; one-fourth against about 30% of men re-addicted in year 1 addicted again in years 2 to 3); the claim uses the figures with stated time frames. The matched civilian comparison group is described but gives no figures in either paper read.
